universetoday.com/articles/unveiling-sta.excerpt: In 1985, the physicist Heinz R. Pagels wrote, "Stars are like animals in the wild. We may see the youung, but never the actual birth, which is a veiled and secret event." In the decades since then, astronomers have drawn closer and closer to figuring out what actually goes in the veiled stellar nurseries throughout the Universe. The tale of starbirth we know today invokes collapse of clouds of gas and dust into prestellar cores, but it still has many unknowns, such as the role of magnetic fields in the clouds where stars are born.

universetoday.com/articles/dead-planets-.title: Dead Planets Orbiting a Dead Star
universetoday.com/articles/dead-planets-.excerpt: When a star like our Sun reaches its end, it becomes a kind of zombie star called a white dwarf. These bodies have left fusion behind and will radiate only remnant heat for a long, long time. Before they become white dwarfs, they expand, engulf, and destroy any nearby planets. Astronomers have spotted a debris disk around a white dwarf, made from the dust of destroyed planets. Observations show that two new resurrected planets have formed in this disk, creating dead planets orbiting a dead star.

phys.org/news/2026-10-childhood-employme.excerpt: Research led by the University of East Anglia (UEA) shows that childhood poverty, poor living conditions and gender can have lasting impacts on employment opportunities and earnings in India.

phys.org/news/2026-10-uv-scans-uncover-n.title: UV scans uncover natural varnish that may have preserved ancient Chauvet Cave drawings
phys.org/news/2026-10-uv-scans-uncover-n.excerpt: Tucked away inside a limestone cave in southeastern France lies some of the oldest artwork in existence. Known as Chauvet Cave, the site is so historically important—and fragile—that its location is kept secret and the cave is locked behind a huge steel door. And now, researchers have devised a technique to safely investigate these artworks and understand the natural varnish that has protected them for centuries. Their findings are published in the journal ACS Omega.

phys.org/news/2026-10-supersonic-strange.title: Supersonic waves could explain the strange orbits of hot Jupiters and Neptunes
phys.org/news/2026-10-supersonic-strange.excerpt: Using advanced new simulations, a team of astronomers in the U.S. has developed a promising new theory for how giant, gaseous exoplanets migrate into stiflingly close orbits around their host stars. Led by J. J. Zanazzi at The Pennsylvania State University, the team showed how both massive "hot Jupiters" and smaller, Neptune-sized planets could migrate from distant, elliptical orbits as they release energy via dramatic shock waves in their outer atmospheres. Their results have been published in The Astrophysical Journal.

phys.org/news/2026-10-adults-craft-susta.excerpt: The creator economy is a growing global industry that Goldman Sachs Research reports could be worth $480 billion by 2027. phys.org/news/2026-10-why-hugs-become-me.title: Why hugs become memorable
phys.org/news/2026-10-why-hugs-become-me.excerpt: A large-scale survey of adults in the U.K. shows that hugs are commonly remembered for comfort, support and understanding, according to a study published in PLOS One by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol, U.K., and colleagues. Notably, individual differences in empathy, attachment patterns in relationships, body perception and everyday hugging experiences were also related to the likelihood of remembering a hug for its positive emotional effect.

phys.org/news/2026-10-climate-amplified-.title: Climate change amplified 2024 European floods more than rainfall, models show
phys.org/news/2026-10-climate-amplified-.excerpt: In September 2024, Storm Boris brought extreme precipitation and severe flooding to large parts of Central and Eastern Europe. Poland, Czechia and Austria were particularly affected. In some areas, several hundred millimeters of rain fell within a few days, and numerous rivers burst their banks.

phys.org/news/2026-10-happy.html.title: How to be happy: Tips from the pioneers of well being research
phys.org/news/2026-10-happy.html.excerpt: Earlier this year, we convened a meeting of some of the most influential figures in modern happiness research to discuss what they had learned in their 600 combined years of research and professional experience.

phys.org/news/2026-10-spider-stephen-col.title: A spider named for Stephen Colbert has a genome about 50% larger than ours
phys.org/news/2026-10-spider-stephen-col.excerpt: Many spiders reach their maximum size about this time of year, having spent the summer eating, which helps explain their starring role in Halloween decorations. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have found that one particular trapdoor spider, Aptostichus stephencolberti, which is about the size of a quarter, is big in another way: It has an outsized genome.

phys.org/news/2026-10-political-polariza.title: How political polarization creates business uncertainty
phys.org/news/2026-10-political-polariza.excerpt: New research by a Florida State University professor in the Herbert Wertheim College of Business finds that America's increasingly polarized political system reaches far beyond the ballot box, creating greater uncertainty and higher costs for companies.

phys.org/news/2026-10-yeast-paired-elect.title: Yeast paired with electricity can convert CO₂ into a chemical used in biodegradable plastics
phys.org/news/2026-10-yeast-paired-elect.excerpt: To limit further climate change, researchers are exploring technologies that can convert atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) into useful products. In collaboration with BOKU University in Vienna (Austria), researchers at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) have demonstrated that electrochemical and microbial processes can be combined to capture CO₂ and produce itaconic acid, a bio-based chemical used in industry. According to the researchers, this new process demonstrates how CO₂ emissions can be converted into sustainable bio-based products, with the potential to produce a wider range of valuable chemicals by using different microorganisms.

phys.org/news/2026-10-elementary-school-.title: Elementary school homework could be reinforcing educational inequality, study suggests
phys.org/news/2026-10-elementary-school-.excerpt: Homework set by elementary schools could be reinforcing educational inequalities by rewarding families who have more time and resources to spend helping their children, new research from the University of Manchester suggests.

phys.org/news/2026-10-islands-harbor-ear.title: Islands harbor nearly 20% of Earth's biodiversity, yet remain overlooked in conservation strategies
phys.org/news/2026-10-islands-harbor-ear.excerpt: Although they account for just 7% of the Earth's land surface, island ecosystems harbor almost 20% of the world's biodiversity. From sea-level rise to biological invasions, islands are facing multiple pressures associated with ongoing global change, and yet they are still overlooked in global biodiversity conservation strategies.

phys.org/news/2026-10-evolutionary-biolo.title: How evolutionary biology became an unwilling ally of the manosphere
phys.org/news/2026-10-evolutionary-biolo.excerpt: From steroid use to "bone smashing", the "looksmaxxing" movement is only the latest example of the manosphere's toxic hold on young people.

phys.org/news/2026-10-simulations-fall-s.title: When simulations fall short, this spectrometer learns for itself
phys.org/news/2026-10-simulations-fall-s.excerpt: An NMR spectrometer can reveal molecular structure down to the atomic level, but weak signals limit what it can see. Now, Aarhus University researchers have used AI to let the spectrometer learn the best pulse sequence directly from the sample.

phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-atom-raw-.title: The hydrogen atom: The raw material of the universe barely exists on Earth—now we've made it in a flask
phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-atom-raw-.excerpt: What do you see when you look up at the night sky? While everyone may have a different answer, the truth is that almost everything out there is hydrogen. The first element in the periodic table is by far the most abundant substance in the cosmos. It's the fuel of stars and the raw material from which the heavier elements were forged over billions of years. Even the sun is, at its core, a furnace for fusing hydrogen atoms together.

phys.org/news/2026-10-vasari-page.html.title: Discovering Vasari beyond the page
phys.org/news/2026-10-vasari-page.html.excerpt: Most students of Renaissance art encounter Giorgio Vasari through a book. His Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, first published in 1550 and expanded in a second edition in 1568, is often considered the first major work of art history, shaping how generations have understood artists such as Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci and Raphael. For centuries, Vasari's reputation has rested largely on his role as the artistic biographer of the Renaissance.

phys.org/news/2026-10-extracellular-vesi.title: Extracellular vesicle discovery may shed light on how cancer spreads
phys.org/news/2026-10-extracellular-vesi.excerpt: A team from the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Center (The Institute) have discovered a new type of extracellular vesicle released by migrating cancer cells, revealing a previously unknown way in which these cells shed their DNA as they move. Published today in the journal Nature Cell Biology, the findings show that these cells release tiny structures called motile vesicles (MoVes), which carry their genetic material, including cancer-associated mutations. The discovery raises important questions about the role these vesicles may play in cancer progression.

phys.org/news/2026-10-motion-electron-ca.title: Slow-motion electron camera reveals light-driven quantum jumps in graphene
phys.org/news/2026-10-motion-electron-ca.excerpt: Using a new slow-motion electron camera, physicists from Regensburg, Marburg and Jülich revealed how intense electric fields drive electrons in graphene, causing them to jump across energy gaps in a seemingly paradoxical manner. This was made possible by a novel combination of laser technology and electron microscopy.

phys.org/news/2026-10-advanced-placement.title: The Advanced Placement gender gap is narrowing but not across all subjects
phys.org/news/2026-10-advanced-placement.excerpt: The gender balance among the top scorers on Advanced Placement exams tends to track the gender balance among students taking those tests, according to a new study led by the University of Georgia.

phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-team-habitabl.title: NASA systems engineering team details Habitable Worlds Observatory mission architecture
phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-team-habitabl.excerpt: Finding an Earth-like world beyond the solar system is the holy grail of exoplanet research, and the field has seen remarkable technological advances in detecting and studying exoplanets since the first confirmed exoplanet around a sun-like star was discovered in 1995. These advances include ground- and space-based telescopes, notably the James Webb Space Telescope. Although astronomers have already directly imaged some exoplanets, directly imaging Earth-like planets around sun-like stars remains a major technological challenge, primarily because these planets are extremely faint compared with their host stars and appear very close to them in the sky.

phys.org/news/2026-10-solar-storm-trigge.title: 2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
phys.org/news/2026-10-solar-storm-trigge.excerpt: The Earth is surrounded by an invisible barrier that was thought to prevent highly energetic electrons from reaching closer to our planet. But in 2024, Japan's Arase space probe detected these electrons well inside the barrier. Now, research led by Nagoya University has found evidence that the electrons were accelerated locally rather than infiltrating from outer radiation belts.

phys.org/news/2026-10-refugees-loss-busi.title: Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
phys.org/news/2026-10-refugees-loss-busi.excerpt: The severity of the losses refugees experience can shape the kinds of businesses they build in a new country, according to a qualitative study by Tilburg University researcher Kurian George and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-10-portable-device-ac.title: Portable device accurately and rapidly detects PFAS in water
phys.org/news/2026-10-portable-device-ac.excerpt: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals known for their exceptional resistance to degradation, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." These persistent substances can accumulate in water, soil and living organisms, raising concerns about their potential impacts on human health and the environment.

phys.org/news/2026-10-gravitational-fiel.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
phys.org/news/2026-10-gravitational-fiel.excerpt: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares.

phys.org/news/2026-10-urban-street-trees.title: Urban street trees lose much of their capacity to cool during droughts
phys.org/news/2026-10-urban-street-trees.excerpt: The combination of heat waves and drought markedly reduces the capacity of street trees to cool the air in Mediterranean cities. The lack of soil moisture severely restricts plant transpiration, reducing the thermal relief provided by these trees during extreme heat events.

phys.org/news/2026-10-global-seed-platfo.title: Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
phys.org/news/2026-10-global-seed-platfo.excerpt: On Oct. 13, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launched the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover.

phys.org/news/2026-10-japan-genome-law-g.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
phys.org/news/2026-10-japan-genome-law-g.excerpt: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.

phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-core-atom.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-core-atom.excerpt: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

space.com/entertainment/space-movies-sho.excerpt: The spoilerific final look at Denis Villeneuve's third and final sci-fi epic is loaded with action and drama that set it apart from Dune: Messiah's pages.

space.com/astronomy/earth/satellites-wat.title: Satellites watch an escaping Antarctic iceberg | Space photo of the day for Oct. 28, 2026
space.com/astronomy/earth/satellites-wat.excerpt: Iceberg A-81 escaping the Weddell Sea and drifting near the edge of South Georgia's underwater shelf.

universetoday.com/articles/betelgeuse-is.title: Betelgeuse Is Disturbed By Its Companion Star
universetoday.com/articles/betelgeuse-is.excerpt: Betelgeuse has a close-orbiting companion that disturbs the red supergiant into an egg-like shape. New observations show how the two stars interact and how this could help explain the varying brightness of Betelgeuse.

universetoday.com/articles/ancient-comet.title: Ancient Comets Carried Organic Compounds, But They Didn't Survive Crashing Into Earth
universetoday.com/articles/ancient-comet.excerpt: Perhaps the biggest mystery we face is life on Earth started. One hypothesis says that comets, which are known to carry important chemicals in abiogenesis, delivered these compounds to Earth, leading to the appearance of life. But new research concludes that that is highly unlikely.

universetoday.com/articles/the-rubin-obs.title: The Rubin Observatory Finds Its First Dwarf Planet Candidate
universetoday.com/articles/the-rubin-obs.excerpt: The Vera Rubin Observatory found a distant Solar System object before its decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time even got started. The object is a dwarf planet candidate named 2026 ED138, and if confirmed, it will be one of the largest dwarf planets beyond Neptune. It may be up to 1500 km in diameter.

universetoday.com/articles/the-leap-seco.title: The Leap Second is History. Long Live the 'Leap Hour'
universetoday.com/articles/the-leap-seco.excerpt: Time and time-keeping is a hot topic once again, as many of us ‘fall back’ to Standard Time this coming weekend. Another time-related dilemma was also addressed this month, when a key conference did away with the leap second and the alignment of Universal Time (UT1) with Universal Coordinated Time (UTC). Somewhere off in the distant future, we’ll need to add minutes to the clock to come back into sync, up to and perhaps including a 'leap hour.' Accounting for time is fascinating (if a bit break-brain breaking) stuff to consider.

phys.org/news/2026-10-covid-era-snap-eme.title: End of COVID-era SNAP emergency food assistance linked to increased child maltreatment rates
phys.org/news/2026-10-covid-era-snap-eme.excerpt: A new study has found that in U.S. counties that ended COVID-19 pandemic-era Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments, child maltreatment rates went up. The findings from the study in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine suggest that changes to food assistance programs have consequences that extend beyond food security and also affect child and family well-being.

phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic-climate.title: Optimistic climate futures for local communities in the UK imagined in a new report
phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic-climate.excerpt: A new report co-authored by researchers from the University of York and WWF highlights how local communities across the U.K. imagine positive, sustainable, and resilient futures for the places where they live and work.

phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-ocean-linke.title: How the Indian Ocean is linked to Europe's early-winter rain and storms
phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-ocean-linke.excerpt: When we think about Europe's winter weather, the Indian Ocean is probably not the first place we look. We might picture Atlantic storms, cold air arriving from the north or rain sweeping across the Mediterranean. In my research, however, I look at how these familiar weather systems fit into a much larger climate system. My colleagues and I asked whether an ocean thousands of kilometers away could leave a detectable signature on Europe's early winter.

phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-lighthouse.title: The phantom lighthouse: New research explains one of Australia's strangest illusions
phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-lighthouse.excerpt: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The first was built in 1873, but was decommissioned in 1995 when the second took over the job of warning ships off the reef. Visitors to the island, however, regularly report seeing signs of a third lighthouse. At night the beams of a nonexistent phantom lighthouse are seen far off, shining on the horizon.

phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-metal-la.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-metal-la.excerpt: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-magnetism-r.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-magnetism-r.excerpt: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place.

phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolecular-cro.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolecular-cro.excerpt: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-architec.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-architec.excerpt: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

phys.org/news/2026-10-difference-brittle.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
phys.org/news/2026-10-difference-brittle.excerpt: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-decoding-cell-c.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-decoding-cell-c.excerpt: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

phys.org/news/2026-10-chornobyl-dog-popu.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
phys.org/news/2026-10-chornobyl-dog-popu.excerpt: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes.

phys.org/news/2026-10-gen-artificial-int.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
phys.org/news/2026-10-gen-artificial-int.excerpt: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient.

phys.org/news/2026-10-radical-paths-ray-.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
phys.org/news/2026-10-radical-paths-ray-.excerpt: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites.

phys.org/news/2026-10-schools-affected-p.title: Schools increasingly affected by poor air quality as wildfire smoke becomes more common
phys.org/news/2026-10-schools-affected-p.excerpt: American children are increasingly exposed to air pollution as wildfire smoke becomes more common, and some schools and child care centers struggle to keep indoor breathing conditions clean, a new national study shows.

phys.org/news/2026-10-medieval-ghost-sto.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon‑stealing spirits
phys.org/news/2026-10-medieval-ghost-sto.excerpt: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature.

phys.org/news/2026-10-rarely-deep-sea-ba.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
phys.org/news/2026-10-rarely-deep-sea-ba.excerpt: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head.

phys.org/news/2026-10-drones-weather-acc.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
phys.org/news/2026-10-drones-weather-acc.excerpt: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

phys.org/news/2026-10-gibberellin-reveal.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
phys.org/news/2026-10-gibberellin-reveal.excerpt: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant.

phys.org/news/2026-10-year-mystery-ident.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
phys.org/news/2026-10-year-mystery-ident.excerpt: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

phys.org/news/2026-10-tissue-atlas-aims-.title: New tissue atlas aims to help AI understand cancer
phys.org/news/2026-10-tissue-atlas-aims-.excerpt: How cells are arranged within tissue can reveal as much about disease as the cells themselves. When doctors examine a cancer tumor, for example, they don't just look at which cells are present; they also want to know how those cells are arranged and how they interact with each other. That's because the way cancer cells interact with neighboring immune cells can offer important clues about how a disease develops or responds to treatment.

phys.org/news/2026-10-relocating-amphibi.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
phys.org/news/2026-10-relocating-amphibi.excerpt: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way.

phys.org/news/2026-10-sun-outer-magnetic.title: Sun's outer magnetic field mapped in 3D for the first time
phys.org/news/2026-10-sun-outer-magnetic.excerpt: A team of researchers has produced the first global, three-dimensional estimates of the sun's magnetic field, including the area beyond the sun's visible edge. This marks a step toward more accurate models of solar activity—and ultimately, better predictions of solar magnetic eruptions, which are the root cause of extreme space weather that can impact critical infrastructure technologies on Earth.

phys.org/news/2026-10-physics-ai-tool-ai.title: A new physics-informed AI tool aims to predict wildfire spread in real time and assist wildfire response
phys.org/news/2026-10-physics-ai-tool-ai.excerpt: A new AI system that NYU Fire Research Group describes as a digital twin of an active wildfire has, in early testing, shown the ability to forecast how a fire will spread in near real time.

phys.org/news/2026-10-customizable-dna-d.title: Customizable DNA labels can selectively guide drug carriers to cancer cells
phys.org/news/2026-10-customizable-dna-d.excerpt: Cells naturally send tiny packages to one another to share information. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have developed a simple, low-cost way to turn those packages into drug carriers that can deliver treatments directly to cancer cells, potentially improving effectiveness while reducing side effects.

phys.org/news/2026-10-humidity-pollutant.title: Humidity can change how smoke pollutants transform after dark
phys.org/news/2026-10-humidity-pollutant.excerpt: What happens to smoke particles after sunset can depend strongly on something as familiar as the amount of water in the air. New research from Md. Sohel Rana and Marcelo I. Guzman at the University of Kentucky shows that relative humidity can redirect the chemical pathways involved in the nighttime oxidation of catechol, a phenolic compound associated with biomass burning.

phys.org/news/2026-10-forgotten-holocaus.title: 'Let nothing be forgotten': Holocaust survivors' memorial books honored lives lost and vibrant hometowns
phys.org/news/2026-10-forgotten-holocaus.excerpt: My grandmother was a Holocaust survivor from Kostopol, Ukraine. Years after she passed away, I was trying to learn more about her life before the war—something I knew very little about. When I found a book called "Sefer Kostopol"—Hebrew for "Book of Kostopol"—I hoped to find her among its pages.

phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists-million.title: Scientists count more than 2 million eels on one underwater mountain

Every year, it is the site of an enormous gathering of basketwork eels (Diastobranchus capensis) for reasons unknown, although most likely to spawn. The numbers are huge, but they have never been quantified.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027.title: Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027.excerpt: Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027.excerpt: Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261027.excerpt: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.

space.com/space-exploration/private-spac.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.

universetoday.com/articles/moon-habitats.title: Moon Habitats May Use Layered Mylar to Block Extreme Heat
universetoday.com/articles/moon-habitats.excerpt: Living on the Moon, with either trained astronauts or regular civilians, could become a regular occurrence in the near future. However, it’s easier said than done, as scientists and engineers continue developing new and advanced ways for protecting humans in the harsh lunar environment, which contrasts the mild and habitable temperatures of the Earth. The most important aspect is focusing on keeping humans alive, and this includes temperature regulation within the habitats. However, how can you maintain temperature regulation while being flexible enough to withstand physical changes like moving, handling, and compression and expansion?

universetoday.com/articles/virgin-galact.title: Virgin Galactic Flies Next-Gen Space Plane to New Home With New Name
universetoday.com/articles/virgin-galact.excerpt: Virgin Galactic is back in the spaceflight spotlight with the unveiling of a shiny new object: an updated Delta-class suborbital space plane with an exotic name.

universetoday.com/articles/nasas-new-uv-.title: NASA's New UV Space Telescope Will Launch in 2031
universetoday.com/articles/nasas-new-uv-.excerpt: NASA has committed to launching a new, more powerful UV space telescope. Named UVEX, the UltraViolet EXplorer, it will launch in 2031. It's about 100 times more powerful than its predecessor, GALEX, whose mission ended in 2013. UVEX will perform a survey in UV that will complement infrared surveys by other telescopes.

sciencenews.org/article/mars-cloud-homog.title: A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics
sciencenews.org/article/mars-cloud-homog.excerpt: Everyday Earth clouds get their start with a bit of salt or dust. Not so the Red Planet's Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, computer models suggest.

phys.org/news/2026-10-modest-gamma-ray-d.title: Modest gamma-ray flash followed by dazzling afterglow points to powerful stellar jet viewed off-axis
phys.org/news/2026-10-modest-gamma-ray-d.excerpt: A cosmic explosion that announced itself with a modest flash of gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. An international team of astronomers now finds evidence that the surprising mismatch comes down to perspective: Earth was outside the most intensely beamed light from the explosion.

phys.org/news/2026-10-indoor-air-quality.title: Indoor plants could improve air quality and cooling
phys.org/news/2026-10-indoor-air-quality.excerpt: In a study published in Eco-Environment and Health, a team of 35 international experts led by Surrey's Global Centre for Clean Air Research (GCARE) reviewed several studies from across the world on the performance of indoor greenery.

phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-ammonia-l.title: Using hydrogen to spark ammonia engines into life
phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-ammonia-l.excerpt: "Ammonia was first used as a fuel during World War II, when gasoline was hard to get hold of," explains David Emberson, associate professor at NTNU's Department of Marine Technology.

phys.org/news/2026-10-saharan-bacteria-a.title: Saharan dust carries desert bacteria across the Atlantic to Amazon rainforest
phys.org/news/2026-10-saharan-bacteria-a.excerpt: Viewed under a microscope, the air above the Amazon rainforest teems with activity. It is full of pollen, fungal spores, tiny plant particles and bacteria. Normally, the composition of this bioaerosol community is quite stable. A team that included researchers from the University of Graz, the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz and Brazilian partner institutions has now shown that microorganisms are transported across the Atlantic along with desert dust from the Sahara.

phys.org/news/2026-10-children-academic-.title: Children need to learn to swim for academic and social milestones, rather than just fitness, research suggests
phys.org/news/2026-10-children-academic-.excerpt: With family budgets stretched ever tighter, swimming lessons can be one of the first expenses to be cut back—but with research showing swimming helps children not just physically but developmentally, researchers are calling for greater government support.

phys.org/news/2026-10-struggling-career-.title: Struggling with your career? This psychological intervention may help
phys.org/news/2026-10-struggling-career-.excerpt: Job loss and career uncertainty can take a toll that extends well beyond the workplace. New research suggests that a psychological intervention based on the principles of acceptance and commitment therapy, or ACT, may help individuals navigate work-related challenges while improving well-being and reducing psychological distress.

phys.org/news/2026-10-amino-acid-boosts-.title: Amino acid boosts last-resort antibiotic's effectiveness
phys.org/news/2026-10-amino-acid-boosts-.excerpt: Worldwide, antibiotic resistance is associated with millions of deaths every year, and the World Health Organization warns that the number of resistant infections is rising. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used when other treatments fail, but rates of colistin-resistant infections are rising as well, putting people at even greater risk and increasing the urgency for new therapeutic approaches.

phys.org/news/2026-10-children-brunt-cli.title: Children bear the brunt of climate change, warns new report
phys.org/news/2026-10-children-brunt-cli.excerpt: Climate change is posing an increasing threat to the health and well-being of children and young people in Australia and New Zealand, with rising exposure to heat waves and widespread climate-related distress among young Australians, according to the annual MJA–Lancet Countdown Oceania report.

phys.org/news/2026-10-smaller-ants-devot.title: Smaller ants devote more of their resting energy budget to their brains
phys.org/news/2026-10-smaller-ants-devot.excerpt: The energy required for brains of different sizes to function could play a role in how different species evolved over time. While the energetic costs of brains have long been deemed important in evolution, direct measurements of the rate at which the brains of different species consume energy, also known as brain metabolic rates (MRs), remain scarce.

phys.org/news/2026-10-individual-based-b.title: First individual-based model of basking sharks replicates complicated social and environmental drivers of behavior
phys.org/news/2026-10-individual-based-b.excerpt: A new study published in Individual-Based Ecology presents the first individual-based model (IBM) of basking shark behavior.

phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-polls-trustwort.title: Q&A: Are polls trustworthy?
phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-polls-trustwort.excerpt: In the final stretch to the midterm elections, polls have come out tracking candidates' likelihood of victory at the local, state and federal levels. According to Tim Servinsky, project manager at Penn State Harrisburg's Center for Survey Research, polls built with the right questions and asked to the right population can be accurate and a critical tool for policymakers. However, particularly in the context of political polling, there are important details to keep in mind when reading and interpreting the most recent polling projections.

phys.org/news/2026-10-electricity-uncert.title: How to keep electricity costs down amid uncertain federal policy
phys.org/news/2026-10-electricity-uncert.excerpt: Keeping the lights on nationwide is a feat of engineering that depends on millions of miles of power lines and thousands of power-generation plants.

phys.org/news/2026-10-prosecutors-invoke.title: Prosecutors invoke gender stereotypes in capital cases against women
phys.org/news/2026-10-prosecutors-invoke.excerpt: In 2001, Brenda Andrew was convicted of murdering her husband, and in 2004 she was sentenced to death.

phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-oceans-car.title: As ancient oceans warmed, carbon export and fish productivity surged
phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-oceans-car.excerpt: Ocean fish stocks have been increasingly exploited over time, and remote sensing shows they have declined in the open ocean over the last three decades, particularly in the tropics. esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Scienc.excerpt: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.

universetoday.com/articles/colliding-dwa.title: Colliding Dwarf Planets Created a 'Cat's Tail' 1,000 Astronomical Units Long
universetoday.com/articles/colliding-dwa.excerpt: The Beta Pictoris system is only about 63 light years away. At only about 23 million years old, it's a sort of analogue for our Solar System when it was much younger. Observations show an elongated dust feature named the 'Cat's Tail' that has puzzled researchers. New research says it's the result of two colliding dwarf planets, something that was sure to have happened in our Solar System when it was young.

phys.org/news/2026-10-lab-aged-microplas.excerpt: A newly published study advances our knowledge of how microplastics may age in the environment and whether they stick to other contaminants as they do so. Microplastics (MPs) are tiny plastic pieces that measure less than 5 millimeters (about 0.2 inches) in length. The study looked at the aging of MPs made of three common polymer chemicals—polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate and polypropylene—to see if they changed as they aged and how that affected nearby contaminants.

phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-tool-scientists.excerpt: A handful of soil holds a crowded world of bacteria, fungi and other organisms. Scientists can collect their DNA, but much of it remains difficult to identify. Now, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and partner institutions have developed an artificial intelligence tool that helps make sense of this genetic puzzle.

By combining X-ray absorption spectroscopy with data analysis, the researchers separated the weak signals of interfacial water from those of the much larger amount of surrounding water.

phys.org/news/2026-10-tool-combines-algo.title: New travel tool combines three algorithms to tailor destination recommendations
phys.org/news/2026-10-tool-combines-algo.excerpt: Researchers have developed a tourist recommendation system combining three algorithms to help travelers find destinations suited to their preferences, budgets and travel routes. phys.org/news/2026-10-machine-safer-citi.title: Using machine learning to build safer cities
phys.org/news/2026-10-machine-safer-citi.excerpt: In eThekwini, researchers have harnessed machine learning and satellite data to spot the city's most landslide-prone zones. phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-billion-year-.excerpt: Scientists at the University of New Mexico have played a key role in identifying a rare, 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite that provides new evidence that the red planet may have once had a wetter, Earth-like environment.

phys.org/news/2026-10-electrical-guardra.title: Electrical guardrails for charge carriers: A new approach to harness graphene for solar cells
phys.org/news/2026-10-electrical-guardra.excerpt: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in which electrons can move with high mobility, making it promising for high-speed electronic components. Yet it is not very efficient at converting light into electricity. While light absorbed by graphene does excite electrons, leaving behind positively charged carriers called 'holes,' the absorbed light energy cannot be harnessed effectively unless electrons and holes are separated and directed to different contacts.

phys.org/news/2026-10-faraway-tectonic-g.title: Faraway tectonic forces may have accelerated the Gulf of California rifting
phys.org/news/2026-10-faraway-tectonic-g.excerpt: When the Baja California peninsula broke from mainland Mexico nearly 12 million years ago, it gave rise to the Gulf of California. New research suggests that this process of continental rifting was greatly accelerated due to tectonic forces on the opposite side of the Pacific Ocean.

Their functions depend on their amino acid composition and three-dimensional structures. However, early proteins may have evolved when fewer amino acid types were available than those used by most modern proteins.

phys.org/news/2026-10-asteroids-venturin.title: Asteroids venturing near white dwarfs don't break directly into dust, study reveals

The challenge comes when they want to distinguish many reactions on the same electrode. After more than a decade of trying to overcome that limitation, Ravi Saraf and his Nebraska Engineering graduate students have demonstrated a way to quantify many reactions on the same electrode without sacrificing extraordinary sensitivity.

phys.org/news/2026-10-protein-mrna-decod.title: A protein that regulates mRNA decoding can itself be regulated with implications for understanding cancer
phys.org/news/2026-10-protein-mrna-decod.excerpt: Decoding of messenger RNA (mRNA) occurs during translation, the vital cellular process that builds proteins. Errors in this process are known to lead to cancer growth. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital identified how one factor involved in mRNA decoding can be altered, identifying potential cancer origins and new targets for KRAS-related treatment resistance. The results are published in Nature Cell Biology.

phys.org/news/2026-10-el-nio-monterey-ba.title: Researchers observe the arrival of El Niño in Monterey Bay

These data are integral to understanding our changing ocean and underpin the institute's efforts to monitor the impacts of the incoming El Niño, which has been predicted to be among the strongest since the beginning of modern oceanography.

They are commonly maintained by powerful winds that push newly formed ice away from the coast, repeatedly exposing the ocean to the freezing Antarctic atmosphere.

phys.org/news/2026-10-chemical-recycling.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
phys.org/news/2026-10-chemical-recycling.excerpt: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

phys.org/news/2026-10-borneo-wildfires-i.title: Borneo's wildfires could have a lasting impact on orangutans
phys.org/news/2026-10-borneo-wildfires-i.excerpt: Indonesia is battling one of its most severe wildfire seasons in over a decade, as intense El Niño conditions fuel widespread drought. Peatlands across West, Central and South Kalimantan are smoldering underground, releasing smoke haze that threatens human health and the environment.

universetoday.com/articles/how-you-squee.excerpt: Studying the interiors of planets is essential for understanding planetary formation, evolution, and their ability to potentially host life as we know it. To accomplish this, researchers use a combination of Earth as an analog, computer models, meteorites, and data collected from other planetary bodies for studying their interior compositions. As a result, scientists have determined that the elements of magnesium and silicon are the most abundant planetary building blocks. And, under extreme pressures like the interior mantle of our planet, it forms magnesium oxide (MgO) crystals. But how does this same process occur under different pressures and temperatures on other planets like gas giants and larger rocky exoplanets called super-Earths?

phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-copper-hin.excerpt: Copper is essential for making bronze, which shaped tools, weapons and ornaments across Bronze Age Europe. While many Bronze Age mines have been identified throughout Europe, researchers are still trying to pin down which of them were most active at different times and how far their copper traveled. New research, published in the journal Antiquity, suggests that a series of mines in modern-day Spain and Portugal may have been an important source of copper in the Late Bronze Age, with some of that copper ending up as far away as Scandinavia.

phys.org/news/2026-10-gamma-ray-powerhou.title: A gamma-ray powerhouse's smoking gun? Gas trail points to microquasar jets
phys.org/news/2026-10-gamma-ray-powerhou.excerpt: In 2016, a binary star system emitting unusually strong gamma rays was discovered in our galactic neighborhood. Now, astronomers have found the smoking gun, or rather, a smoking trail of cool molecular gas that suggests jets emanating from a microquasar—one of the few known outside the Milky Way—are responsible.

phys.org/news/2026-10-bonus-employees-co.title: The bonus that makes employees more committed
phys.org/news/2026-10-bonus-employees-co.excerpt: Offer your employees money to quit and the ones who say no will work harder as a result. Researchers at the University of Waterloo, Wilfrid Laurier University and McMaster University set out to test whether pay-to-quit programs work as intended. Their results confirmed they do and revealed a benefit that nobody anticipated.

phys.org/news/2026-10-transcription-chro.title: Different transcription systems shape chromatin behavior in distinct nuclear regions
phys.org/news/2026-10-transcription-chro.excerpt: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which are further organized into chromatin. Chromatin has traditionally been divided into transcriptionally active euchromatin and relatively inactive heterochromatin. However, chromatin is not a fixed structure. Nucleosomes continuously move within the nucleus, and this motion is closely related to the physical organization and function of the genome.

phys.org/news/2026-10-companies-climate-.title: Companies' progress on climate reporting gets lost in the average
phys.org/news/2026-10-companies-climate-.excerpt: Companies are increasingly expected to explain the climate risks and how they are responding. CDP, formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project, is a nonprofit that collects and scores corporate environmental disclosures, including emissions data, climate risks and governance practices. How has CDP's average score changed year by year, and does that trend capture the progress of companies that have disclosed consistently for many years?

phys.org/news/2026-10-supercharged-molec.title: Supercharged 'molecule highway' membrane that speeds water transport could transform industrial processing
phys.org/news/2026-10-supercharged-molec.excerpt: New membrane technology delivering faster and more precise molecule separation could improve the efficiency and sustainability of energy-intensive industrial processes—from purifying chemicals and recovering valuable resources to producing sustainable fuels.

phys.org/news/2026-10-stem-cells-fruit-f.title: Pulling the strings: How stem cells in the developing fruit fly brain organize their DNA from outside the nucleus
phys.org/news/2026-10-stem-cells-fruit-f.excerpt: Cells are very particular about the proper locations of their contents. For example, DNA is packaged in the nucleus in a highly specific way, but researchers are still trying to understand how this happens. For stem cells in the brain of a larval fruit fly—a model organism used to study processes such as early development—the DNA is organized so that the center of each strand, called the centromere, is at the top of the nucleus.

phys.org/news/2026-10-fish-schools-sync-.title: How fish schools swim in sync may come down to following one influential neighbor
phys.org/news/2026-10-fish-schools-sync-.excerpt: Fish schools are a marvel of navigation. They move in concert without any one fish leading the way. Instead, their coordinated movements arise from individual fish continually adjusting their movements based on their neighbors. But how much of this social information each fish processes at once is less well understood.

phys.org/news/2026-10-global-ocellated-l.title: Global change may alter how ocellated lizards move between shelters, food and predators
phys.org/news/2026-10-global-ocellated-l.excerpt: Global change is also affecting the behavior and mobility of the ocellated lizard, a reptile typical of Mediterranean ecosystems. This species—the largest lizard on the Iberian Peninsula—could experience changes in its ability to move efficiently between shelters and feeding areas, escape predators and interact with its natural environment. This is the conclusion of a paper published in the Journal of Animal Ecology led by researcher Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou, from the Faculty of Biology and the Biodiversity Research Institute (IRBio) at the University of Barcelona.

phys.org/news/2026-10-discovery-bromochl.title: Discovery of bromochloropyrene reveals unexpected biological properties
phys.org/news/2026-10-discovery-bromochl.excerpt: Environmental pollutants containing chlorine or bromine have been widely studied, but compounds containing both elements have remained largely unexplored. Researchers have now detected bromochloropyrene in industrial soils and harbor sediments, investigated its breakdown under simulated sunlight, and measured its activity through a biological receptor linked to toxic effects. The findings reveal distinct environmental and biological properties, highlighting the need to investigate other mixed-halogen pollutants and improve future environmental monitoring and risk assessment.

phys.org/news/2026-10-cages-protein-kill.title: Researchers create light-activated cages for 'protein killer' molecules
phys.org/news/2026-10-cages-protein-kill.excerpt: Researchers have created a molecular "cage" that keeps protein-degrading drug molecules inactive until they are exposed to low-energy red light. The technology, called RuPHOTACs, controls when and where these molecules become active, which could help scientists develop treatments that destroy specific proteins while limiting unwanted effects elsewhere.

phys.org/news/2026-10-grades-schools-swe.excerpt: Grades from compulsory school determine which pupils are accepted into popular upper secondary programs. A new thesis from Uppsala University shows that pupils at for-profit independent schools have, on average, higher grades than would statistically be expected given their backgrounds. The findings suggest that grading is more generous in independent schools and that the differences in grades may give pupils from high-income households a greater advantage in the competition for places at upper secondary school, at the expense of other pupils.

phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists-millise.excerpt: Nitrogen dioxide is a harmful gas that requires sensitive detection. Researchers used intense light pulses lasting 10 milliseconds to make molybdenum disulfide flakes and anchor isolated metal atoms in one step. Adding platinum improved the material's room-temperature response to nitrogen dioxide, reaching 100.8% at 400 parts per billion and a detection limit of 17.2 parts per billion. This approach could support advanced gas sensors and applications in catalysis and energy technologies.

But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Mars’ climate history?

universetoday.com/articles/ceres-water-i.excerpt: The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an “asteroid” since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceres’ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceres’ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several “bright spots”, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceres’ formation and evolution?

universetoday.com/articles/space-outpost.title: Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI
universetoday.com/articles/space-outpost.excerpt: NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972. But the famed agency has no intention of stopping there, as they plan to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon through a slow and meticulous process involving power, resource extraction, and habitat technologies. However, with the soaring use of artificial intelligence (AI) in our everyday lives, how could this emerging technology be used to identify new landing sites for future outposts on the Moon and possibly Mars?

phys.org/news/2026-10-year-mummy-yields-.title: 2,700-year-old mummy head yields first molecular evidence linking aloe to Egyptian embalming
phys.org/news/2026-10-year-mummy-yields-.excerpt: What materials did ancient Egyptians use to preserve the dead, and how can their composition still be investigated thousands of years later? An interdisciplinary team at Marburg University has combined modern natural product analysis with Egyptology and the history of pharmacy to investigate these questions.

phys.org/news/2026-10-ice-scientists-par.title: Breaking the ice: Scientists use attracting particles to form an anti-spin ice
phys.org/news/2026-10-ice-scientists-par.excerpt: In a recent Nature Communications study, researchers have reported the realization of an anti-spin ice, a system that does the opposite of conventional spin ices by breaking the ice rule that governs them.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031.excerpt: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031.excerpt: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030.excerpt: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030.title: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030.excerpt: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.

livescience.com/space/astronomy/webb-and.excerpt: The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

space.com/space-exploration/missions/nas.excerpt: It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where the Swift observatory will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.

space.com/stargazing/5-bright-planets-to.title: 5 bright planets to spot in November — when and where to see them
space.com/stargazing/5-bright-planets-to.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.

astronomy.com/observing/the-sky-today-su.excerpt: Looking for a sky event this week? earthsky.org/space/did-comets-seed-life-.excerpt: Did comets seed life on Earth? It's unlikely, a new study from the University of Cambridge says. It would have been a very rare occurrence. The post Did comets seed life on Earth? A new study says — probably not first appeared on EarthSky .

earthsky.org/space/black-holes-split-ent.excerpt: Black holes sometimes merge. But could 1 split into 2 or more? A new study explores the conditions that might allow it, including extremely rapid rotation. The post Do black holes split into smaller black holes? first appeared on EarthSky .

9.headline: Ultracold Rubidium Atoms Mimic Schwinger Pair Production
9.summary: Researchers used an optical lattice of ultracold rubidium atoms to simulate the elusive Schwinger effect, revealing how mass and field strength control pair creation.
highlights: Ultracold rubidium atoms were arranged in a one‑dimensional optical lattice to represent a false vacuum
Tuning the simulated particle mass and background electric field altered the observed pair‑production rate
Quantum gas microscope imaging captured real‑time dynamics of the simulated particle‑antiparticle creation

7.headline: Delayed Rise of Lyman Continuum Escape in Bursty High‑Redshift Galaxies
7.summary: Simulations show that Lyman continuum escape fractions peak about 16 Myr after star‑formation bursts, especially in massive early galaxies.
highlights: Typical LyC escape lag is ~16 Myr with peak correlations of 0.4‑0.6 in massive haloes
Delay scales as M★⁻⁰·¹⁹ and Mhalo⁻⁰·²⁷, lengthening for lower‑mass systems
Hα‑to‑UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed link to LyC escape, offering an observable tracer

15.headline: Astrolabe Surrogate Generates Full‑Resolution Cosmology Simulations via Flow Matching
15.summary: Astrolabe uses a flow‑matching transformer to emulate particle‑level cosmology, delivering accurate large‑scale structure without voxel resolution limits.
highlights: Acts directly on 6N phase‑space coordinates of individual particles
Employs a hybrid transformer where each particle cross‑attends to multiscale field tokens
Matches physical flow using approximate COLA coordinates, preserving momentum and mass
Reproduces power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity and density profiles in Lambda‑CDM tests
Generalizes to dark‑acoustic oscillation initial conditions and scales to TNG50‑3‑dark size

3.headline: Vienna Researchers Unveil First Self-Stabilizing Thorium‑229 Nuclear Clock
3.summary: A team at TU Wien built a self‑stabilizing nuclear clock using thorium‑229 nuclei, achieving a precision of one‑second error over 30 million years.
highlights: The clock uses a laser‑driven transition in thorium‑229 nuclei to lock its frequency
It operates autonomously for over 24 hours without an external atomic reference
Measured relative precision reaches 10⁻¹⁵, far surpassing typical atomic clocks

8.headline: Rare FN1 Mutation Shields APOE ε4 Carriers from Alzheimer’s Brain Damage
8.summary: Scientists identified a protective FN1 mutation that limits fibrotic buildup around brain vessels, preserving blood‑brain barrier integrity in APOE ε4 carriers into their 80s.
highlights: APOE ε4 drives excess fibronectin accumulation around cerebral blood vessels
A rare FN1 mutation reduces fibronectin deposition and prevents barrier leakage
Single‑cell and spatial analyses confirmed the mechanism in mouse, zebrafish, and human tissue
Findings published in Nature Aging suggest new therapeutic targets for early Alzheimer’s intervention

microblazar_discovery.headline: Astronomers Spot First Microblazar Inside Milky Way Pointing Toward Earth
microblazar_discovery.summary: A tiny blazar, IR 18293‑0941, has been identified in our galaxy, offering a fast‑forward view of jet physics and a possible source of ultrahigh‑energy particles.
highlights: IRAS 18293‑0941 exhibits a one‑sided bright radio jet, the hallmark of a blazar.
Multi‑wavelength data from three observatories confirmed the source lies within the Milky Way.
The jet’s opposite‑directed shock may power the nearby ultrahigh‑energy particle hotspot.
The findings are detailed in a forthcoming Astronomy & Astrophysics paper after two decades of searching.

first_stars_simulations.headline: MEGATRON Simulations Show First Stars Light Up Universe and Seed Elements
first_stars_simulations.summary: Ultra‑detailed MEGATRON simulations reveal how the earliest stars illuminated the dark cosmos and forged carbon, oxygen and iron that later formed planets and life.
highlights: MEGATRON links JWST galaxy observations with chemical fingerprints in ancient Milky Way stars
Simulations track gas dynamics, starlight, and element enrichment from pristine gas to supernovae
High‑resolution models capture gas structures missed by simpler approaches

ocean_warming_method.headline: New Method Shows Double-Digit Gaps Between Ocean Warming and Climate Models
ocean_warming_method.summary: Researchers at the University of Bonn combined buoy data with satellite sea‑level measurements to reveal that individual ocean basins warm up to double‑digit percentages more than climate models predict.
highlights: Indian Ocean absorbed unusually large heat from 2005‑2015
Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans each took roughly one‑third of extra heat over the past 20 years
Method calculates regional thermal‑expansion coefficients, correcting a common uniform‑assumption error

mirror_image_crystals_reverse_the_direct.headline: Mirror‑Image 2D Perovskite Crystals Reverse Light‑Driven Spin Currents
mirror_image_crystals_reverse_the_direct.summary: Researchers at Science Tokyo showed that bulk circular photogalvanic effect in chiral 2D hybrid perovskites flips direction with light handedness, confirming a bulk origin.
highlights: Circular photogalvanic effect (CPGE) observed in 2D organic‑inorganic hybrid perovskite crystals
Photocurrent direction reverses when using right‑ or left‑handed circularly polarized light at normal incidence
Chiral enantiomeric crystals produce opposite CPGE signs, proving bulk polarity controls the current

embryo_model_validation.headline: University of Sydney devises benchmark to gauge lab‑grown human blastoid fidelity
embryo_model_validation.summary: Researchers created a reference map from over 14,000 single‑cell transcriptomes to objectively assess how closely stem‑cell‑derived blastoid models mimic early human embryos.
highlights: Four leading blastoid protocols were systematically compared against a comprehensive embryonic reference map
Some models reproduced all three major lineages, but none fully recapitulated a natural blastocyst
The computational framework and datasets are publicly released for global benchmarking

sea_monkeys_turbulence_rule_2026.headline: Brine Shrimp Reveal How to Reverse Energy Flow in 2D Turbulence
sea_monkeys_turbulence_rule_2026.summary: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh showed that the orientation of tiny brine shrimp can flip the direction of energy cascade in a two‑dimensional turbulent fluid.
highlights: The shrimp’s swimming angle relative to flow determines whether energy moves from small to large scales or vice‑versa.
A simple angled obstacle or array of rods can steer the energy flux in the laboratory tank.
Numerical simulations by the University of Turin confirmed the experimental inverse cascade effect.
Potential applications include low‑energy pollution control and more efficient mixing in drug design.

scientists_discover_first_type_i_superco.headline: First Type‑I Superconductor YbSb₂ Found to Break Time‑Reversal Symmetry
scientists_discover_first_type_i_superco.summary: Researchers at IISC‑Bhopal demonstrated that YbSb₂, a type‑I superconductor, spontaneously generates internal magnetic fields, revealing broken time‑reversal symmetry.
highlights: YbSb₂ crystals exhibit type‑I magnetic behavior, fully expelling external fields
Muon spin rotation measurements detected spontaneous internal fields below the superconducting transition
The observed symmetry breaking suggests an internally antisymmetric nonunitary triplet (INT) state
Calculations indicate possible gapless Majorana surface modes, hinting at topological superconductivity

animal_evolution_earlier.headline: Animals May Have Originated 200 Million Years Earlier Than Fossils Show
animal_evolution_earlier.summary: A new study using Mongolian microfossils and molecular clocks suggests animal life began 800‑700 million years ago, far before the first clear fossils.
highlights: Mongolian Kheseen Biota, 40 million years younger than Weng'an, lacks animal fossils despite excellent preservation
Molecular‑clock analysis pushes animal origin back by ~200 million years to 800‑700 Ma
Chemical biomarkers hint at sponge‑like organisms existing 650 Ma
Early animals likely small, soft‑bodied, and missed by fossilization during Cryogenian Snowball Earth events

agrivoltaics_magenta_panels.headline: Magenta Solar Panels Boost Broccoli Growth While Generating Renewable Power
agrivoltaics_magenta_panels.summary: Semi‑transparent magenta panels increased broccoli’s sunlight use efficiency 4.5‑fold, matching yields despite a 25‑day longer maturation period.
highlights: Broccoli under magenta panels grew as large as open‑field crops while using sunlight 4.5‑times more efficiently
The 20 m × 20 m prototype generated electricity and filtered blue‑red light to enhance photosynthesis
Two panel transparencies produced similar crop performance, indicating flexibility in design

changes_to_platinum_surface_chemistry_bo.headline: Halide Choice Alters Platinum Surface, Boosts Solar Hydrogen Yield
changes_to_platinum_surface_chemistry_bo.summary: EPFL researchers found that using bromide or iodide precursors for platinum deposition eliminates surface poisoning, raising hydrogen evolution to a 17% quantum yield at 700 nm.
highlights: Chloroplatinate precursors leave Pt–Cl species that poison active sites, suppressing hydrogen production
Bromo- and iodoplatinate precursors reduce more readily, avoiding poisoning and improving performance
Modified Pt surfaces achieve an apparent quantum yield of 17% at 700 nm, among the highest for organic semiconductor nanoparticles

ultrafast_xray_azobenzene_switch.headline: Ultrafast X‑rays Capture First‑Picosecond Shape Shift of Azobenzene
ultrafast_xray_azobenzene_switch.summary: Using PAL‑XFEL, researchers observed that azobenzene’s central nitrogen atoms twist within a few picoseconds after light absorption, while its benzene rings stay nearly static.
highlights: Coordinated motion of the two nitrogen atoms initiates the trans‑to‑cis isomerization
Benzene rings remain largely unchanged during the initial reaction stage
Ultrafast X‑ray liquidography separated azobenzene signal from methanol solvent

enzyme_beads_sustainable_chemistry.headline: Enzyme Beads Offer Storable, Efficient Platform for Sustainable Chemical Production
enzyme_beads_sustainable_chemistry.summary: KIT researchers created millimeter‑sized all‑enzyme beads that act as both catalyst and material, enabling reusable, transportable biocatalysis for fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
highlights: Complementary enzyme binding modules self‑assemble into porous protein beads via freeze‑drying.
Hybrid beads combine enzymes with Escherichia coli cells, retaining activity after five months dry storage.
Beads function in continuous‑flow reactors, demonstrating modular scalability for diverse reactions.

tomato_wilt_virus_clone.headline: Texas A&M Develops First U.S. Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus Clone
tomato_wilt_virus_clone.summary: Researchers at Texas A&M AgriLife Research have engineered the nation’s inaugural infectious clone of tomato spotted wilt virus, enabling faster breeding of resistant tomatoes and peppers.
highlights: The clone reproduces the full‑length TSWV genome as an infectious cDNA copy
It allows unlimited virus production for efficient plant inoculation
Breeders can now screen for resistance traits more rapidly, cutting development time
TSWV causes an estimated $100 million in annual crop losses in the southeastern U.S.

superconductor_vacuum_enhancement.headline: Engineered Vacuum Boosts NbSe₂ Superconductivity by Up to 5.4%
superconductor_vacuum_enhancement.summary: Quantum vacuum fluctuations amplified in a terahertz dark cavity raise the critical temperature of six‑layer NbSe₂ by as much as 5.4%.
highlights: Critical temperature increased by up to 5.4% in a six‑layer NbSe₂ device
Critical current and critical magnetic field show significant enhancement near the transition
Effect peaks at a resonant cavity frequency, confirming coupling to dark‑cavity modes

tlr4_undruggable_site_protein_design.headline: Computer‑Designed Protein Blocks Inflammatory Signaling by Targeting TLR4’s Membrane Core
tlr4_undruggable_site_protein_design.summary: Researchers at Scripps Research created a synthetic protein that binds the transmembrane region of Toll‑like receptor 4, sharply reducing NF‑κB inflammation in human cells.
highlights: Designed protein “Design‑6” showed strongest binding to TLR4’s membrane‑spanning segment and lowered NF‑κB activity.
Computational workflow screened nine candidates, with eight confirming membrane association via a light‑up assay.
Study reveals the transmembrane region as an active driver of TLR4 signaling, opening a new drug‑target class.

chang_e6_magnetic_mineral.headline: Chang’e-6 Lunar Soil Reveals Unexpected Magnetic γ‑Fe Nanoparticles
chang_e6_magnetic_mineral.summary: Scientists analyzing Chang’e-6 impact‑glass samples discovered nanoscale γ‑Fe that preserves a stable magnetic signal, offering a new record of the Moon’s ancient magnetic field.
highlights: γ‑Fe identified for the first time in natural lunar samples
Nanoparticles retain a single‑vortex magnetic state under external fields
Impact‑glass cooling and carbon impurities may stabilize high‑temperature γ‑Fe

true_polar_wander_constraints.headline: Ancient Sea‑Level Maps Reveal Multiple Episodes of Rapid True Polar Wander
true_polar_wander_constraints.summary: Researchers used 10‑million‑year sea‑level reconstructions to identify four intervals of fast true polar wander over the past 320 million years.
highlights: Four rapid true polar wander events detected between 200‑190 Ma, 150‑140 Ma, 100‑90 Ma, and 30‑20 Ma
Sea‑level patterns show simultaneous rises and falls in opposite hemispheres, matching model predictions
Study led by Mathew Domeier at the University of Oslo, published in Science
Digital continental flooding maps provided a novel proxy for tracking mantle‑spin axis shifts

milky_way_progenitor_galaxies.headline: Simulations Reveal Milky Way Began as Thousands of Early Galaxies
milky_way_progenitor_galaxies.summary: New MEGATRON simulations suggest the Milky Way formed from a web of thousands of tiny galaxies, predicting their appearance to Hubble and James Webb telescopes.
highlights: Thousands of proto‑galaxies merged over the first billion years to create today’s spiral disk.
Simulations include detailed non‑equilibrium physics, gravity, radiation and chemistry, a first for Milky Way models.
Population III supernovae explain why iron abundance stops decreasing in the faintest early galaxies.
Model predicts star‑less “galaxies” that still emit light, offering new observational targets for JWST.

resistant_bacteria_vulnerabilities.headline: Targeting Energy, Phage Resistance, and Toxin Loading in Superbugs
resistant_bacteria_vulnerabilities.summary: NTU scientists unveiled a metabolism‑blocking compound for Mycobacterium abscessus, revealed phage‑resistance mechanisms, and mapped the toxin‑loading apparatus of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
highlights: A novel inhibitor binds a pocket in M. abscessus cytochrome b bcc oxidase, cutting ATP production and achieving a 2‑log kill
Loss of glycopeptidolipids drives M. abscessus to a rough, more virulent form that evades bacteriophage attack.
Cryo‑EM revealed the Type VI Secretion System loads toxins into Hcp rings, forming a harpoon‑like tube that delivers multiple

kdm4a_drives_tgct_metastasis.headline: KDM4A fuels testicular germ cell tumor spread via STAT1‑CCL3 signaling
kdm4a_drives_tgct_metastasis.summary: Researchers show that the histone demethylase KDM4A drives metastasis of testicular germ cell tumors by activating STAT1‑dependent CCL3 transcription and the PI3K/AKT pathway.
highlights: KDM4A is uniquely over‑expressed in TGCTs among all histone demethylases
Knocking down KDM4A reduces TGCT cell migration, invasion, and lung metastasis in mice
KDM4A demethylates H3K9me3 at the CCL3 promoter, enabling STAT1‑driven transcription
CCL3 activation triggers PI3K/AKT signaling, promoting focal adhesion turnover
Targeting KDM4A may offer a new therapeutic avenue for metastatic TGCT
